name: Crayon Blue
lede: Crayon Blue is a grayish blue from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, close enough to Slate that the two are barely distinguishable on screen, and the dictionary never explains the crayon reference.

sections.title: A drawing-tool name, unexplained
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul list Crayon Blue at #6C7989 on plate 36, row C, column 5 of their 1930 dictionary, dating its first recorded use to 1926 [1]. The ISCC-NBS circular of 1955 files it as "grayish blue" [1]. Why a muted slate-blue took the name of a wax or pastel crayon is undocumented in the 29 books behind our concordance [1].

In our color graph the nearest named neighbor is [[slate|Slate]], just 2.7 units away, close enough that the two names likely describe the same general shade to most eyes [1]. A little further, at 2.9 units, is [[pompeian-blue|Pompeian Blue]] [1]. The Munsell notation is 3.4PB 4.9/2.7, and the swatch sits with our [[blue|blue]] family, its gray modifier also pulling it toward [[grey|grey]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 1.66% of 23,781 paintings, 395 of them, as photographed, with the within-painting lens counting 146 [2]. That makes it more common than 65% of our named colors [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 1.4% of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 1.8 times the rate its museums would predict [2]. Within a painting it most often sits as a light, in 31% of its 146 appearances [2]. Claude Monet is its most devoted painter, holding it in 4 of 50 works here, 5.6 times the baseline of the museums his paintings come from [2]. It is most over-represented in France, twice the expected rate, 45 of 3,443 French paintings [2]. The earliest match dates to 1424, 506 years before Maerz and Paul recorded the name, a floor rather than a first [2].
